paras: The lynching of James Hicks was the killing of a Black man by Black neighbors near Port Gibson, Mississippi, reported in early May 1888. Accused of attempting to outrage a 7-year-old girl, Hicks was whipped by the girl's father and then shot and hanged by neighbors who judged the whipping insufficient. The story ran as a brief in distant papers, one headed "Summary Punishment."

Hicks, described as "a negro," was accused of attempting to outrage "a little colored girl, 7 years old," on the border of Claiborne and "Caplah" counties; she complained to her parents. Her father pursued and captured him, had him tied to a tree and gave him 200 lashes on his bare back. Hicks was then turned loose and ordered to leave the country.

"The colored people of the neighborhood," the account continued, "were not satisfied with the punishment, and determined to lynch the brute." Hicks had armed himself with an adze, and when the group set on him he split one man's head open, knocked down another and ran. He was brought down by "a load or two of buckshot," dragged to a tree some distance away, hanged and left there.

White residents first learned of the killing when the hanging body was found the next morning. The shorter version of the story said only that the neighborhood's Black residents "took charge of him and after a desperate fight lynched him."
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage, and no attacker is named.

The earliest item found, three sentences in the Lexington, Missouri, Intelligencer on May 5, stated the accusation as fact without comment on the killing. A fuller version appeared on May 9 in the Union County Courier of Elk Point, Dakota Territory, and on May 26 in the Sheridan, Wyoming, Enterprise. The Enterprise set it among unrelated national briefs under the heading "Summary Punishment," and the text called Hicks "the fiend" and "the brute."
The longer items share the same wording, and no Mississippi report was found, so the coverage rests on one repeated account.

reader.title: Lynching of James Hicks
bases: Black residents of the neighborhood set on James Hicks, shot him and hanged his body from a tree on an accusation of attempted outrage, with no officers involved (A1, A2, A3).

Hicks was shot and hanged by 'the colored people of the neighborhood', a group that he fought (striking two men) before being shot, acting without any legal authority because they were 'not satisfied' with the father's whipping as punishment for an alleged attempted outrage (A2, A3); the earlier brief also says the neighborhood's Black residents 'lynched him' (A1). No number is given, so a group of three or more is inferred from the plural wording and the two men he struck plus the shooting.

All three items carry one story: A2 and A3 share the same wording and A1 is a condensed form of it, so they are reprints of one report rather than independent accounts, and no local Mississippi report was found (A1, A2, A3).
